title: Web Linking
summary: This specification defines a model for how web resources relate to each other, called links, and for the type of each relationship, called link relation types. It also defines how to put links in HTTP headers using the Link header field.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8288 defines a common model for links between web resources and a way to carry those links in HTTP headers. Each link identifies its context, its relationship type, its target, and any optional details.

questions: what is the http link header
how does the link header anchor parameter work
how do i register a link relation type
subtitle: A common model for describing links between web resources and serializing them in HTTP headers.

tldr.problem: Different web formats described links in different ways, and HTTP had no common header format for conveying resource relationships.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a link as context, relation type, target, and optional target attributes, then serializes links in the Link header field.
tldr.outcome: It clarifies link and attribute cardinality, header syntax, and parsing guidance. RFC 8288 obsoletes RFC 5988.

today: RFC 8288 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2017. It obsoletes RFC 5988; the unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: A Shared Model for Web Links
sections.content:
A link describes a relationship between two web resources and gives a name to the type of that relationship. HTML and Atom already define links, and this RFC provides a model that can describe links in those formats and potentially others.

It also defines the HTTP Link header field, which carries one or more links in an HTTP message. RFC 8288 obsoletes RFC 5988.
sections.plainLanguage: A link tells a program how one resource relates to another. This RFC gives different web formats a shared way to describe that relationship.

sections.title: The Four Parts of a Link
sections.content:
A link has a context, a relation type, a target, and optional target attributes. Together these state that the context has a resource of a particular relationship at the target, with any stated attributes.

For example, a page can identify another resource as its canonical version and give that resource a media type. The RFC does not set a general ordering for links, nor does it require one link context for every format.
sections.plainLanguage: A link identifies the resource it comes from, the meaning of the relationship, and the resource it points to. Optional attributes add details about the target.

sections.title: Registered and Extension Relation Types
sections.content:
A relation type names the meaning of a link, such as copyright. It describes how the context relates to the target, not the format returned when the target is retrieved.

Registered relation types are tokens listed in the IANA registry and are compared without regard to case. Extension relation types are URIs that identify a relation; clients SHOULD NOT automatically retrieve those URIs. Registration requests need a name, description, and stable, freely available specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The relation type gives the link its meaning, such as identifying a copyright resource. It does not say what file format the target will return.

sections.title: Serializing Links in the Link Header
sections.content:
The Link header contains one or more link values. Each value places a URI reference inside angle brackets, followed by optional semicolon-separated parameters. Recipients MUST accept a parameter value written either as a token or as a quoted string.

The target is the URI reference in brackets. A relative target is resolved according to RFC 3986, without using a base URI from the message body. The link context defaults to the URL of the associated representation and can be changed by the anchor parameter. If an application ignores an anchor, it MUST ignore the entire link rather than use it with a different context.
sections.plainLanguage: A Link header puts the target address in angle brackets and can add parameters after semicolons. The anchor parameter can change which resource the link describes.

sections.title: Relation and Target Parameters
sections.content:
The rel parameter is required and MUST NOT appear more than once in a link value. Its value may contain several relation types, which creates several links with the same context, target, and attributes. The rev parameter for a reverse relationship is deprecated.

The header also defines hreflang, media, title, title*, and type as target attributes. Language and media type values are hints and do not override the corresponding fields in the response. Some parameters have a one-occurrence limit, and applications SHOULD prefer title* when both title forms appear.
sections.plainLanguage: The required rel parameter says what relationship the link represents. Other parameters can suggest the target's language, media, title, or type, but those suggestions do not control the response.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
Link header contents are not inherently private, secure, or protected against alteration. The RFC identifies TLS with HTTP as the end-to-end method for providing these properties.

Applications should consider the risks of automatically following or trusting links. An anchor can assert a relationship that is false or malicious. Link targets and anchor values must be converted from IRIs to URIs for the Link header, which does not support IRIs.
sections.plainLanguage: A Link header can be changed or can point to an untrusted resource. Applications should check links before following them and use protected HTTP when the information needs security.

sections.title: Parsing Guidance and Changes from RFC 5988
sections.content:
Appendix B provides non-normative algorithms for parsing Link headers, their parameters, and quoted strings. These algorithms are advisory and more permissive than the formal syntax; the specification text governs if they differ.

Compared with RFC 5988, this RFC clarifies link cardinality and target-attribute cardinality, changes the default link context to depend on the representation, updates the ABNF for HTTP whitespace, and removes an unused IANA registry. It also adds suggested parsing algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix offers one suggested way to parse Link headers, but it does not override the formal rules. The revision also clarifies how many links and attributes can appear.
